lanes.hillsLocal.note: Eric, 2026-10-31: almost every hill street is two lanes, one each direction. Applied to Local streets in City Fire Zones 2 and 3.

lanes.byClass.note: Total lanes by County CLASS where the City pavement-management lane count is missing.

parking.hills.note: Status quo in Fire Zones 2–3: residents would park on both sides (Eric, 2026-10-31), but each run draws one side only on some blocks (parking.range). The City's curb data or aerial counts would replace this.

parking.flats.note: Placeholder: parking on both sides. Replace with the City's curb data.

parking.parkedCarWidthM.note: 8 ft per parked side, as used by KLD in the SB 99 and AB 747 analyses (SOURCE_NOTES A1).

capacity.speedMph.note: Free-flow speed by road class (hills 20 mph matches AB 747: hills free flow 20 mph or less). Capped by the City network SPEED where known. Replace with KLD's surveyed speeds.

capacity.twoLanePcphPerMph.note: AB 747 Table 2 (HCM 2022): two-lane road capacity = 45 pc/h per mph of free-flow speed, max 1,700 (SOURCE_NOTES B2). Applied per direction.

capacity.multilanePcphPerLane.note: AB 747: 1,900 pc/h per lane for multilane roadways (SOURCE_NOTES B3).

capacity.freewayPcphPerLane.note: AB 747: 2,250 pc/h per lane for freeways at 55 mph (SOURCE_NOTES B3).

capacity.rampPcphPerLane.note: Ramp capacity placeholder; AB 747 uses HCM Exhibit 14-12 by ramp speed.

capacity.steepFactor.note: Flow multiplier on segments whose steep grade (90th percentile of 25 m windows) exceeds steepGradePct. KLD's surveyed speeds would already include grade.

capacity.vehicleSpacingM.note: Road length one queued vehicle occupies (storage).

access.movingLaneM.note: 10 ft minimum viable evacuation travel lane, chosen by KLD with City Public Works and Fire staff (SOURCE_NOTES A2).

access.engineClearM.note: Largest City fire truck is 9.25 ft wide (SB 99 report, SOURCE_NOTES A3); with mirrors it needs the same 10 ft lane.

access.fireCodeClearM.note: 20 ft unobstructed width for fire apparatus access roads, California Fire Code section 503.2.1. Context only: it governs new access roads, not existing streets.

access.engineServiceMin.note: 5-minute fire-station drive-time standard from the City's Standards of Coverage, as used in the SB 99 analysis (SOURCE_NOTES A6).

intersections.note: Total vehicles per hour a node can pass, by the highest road class meeting there. Illustrative. The 2025 study names intersections as the main constraint.

demand.personsPerHousehold.note: 2.37 persons per household (ACS), Evacuation Time Study 2-1, 3-3 (SOURCE_NOTES E5). Converts Genasys zone population estimates to households.

demand.householdsWithoutVehicleShare.note: 7.47% of households have no vehicle (ACS), Time Study Table 3-10 (SOURCE_NOTES E7). Citywide value; AB 747 has it by census tract.

demand.vehiclesTakenShares.note: Of households that drive: 1 vehicle 73.6%, 2 vehicles 14.6%, 3 vehicles 1.3%, 4+ 0.5% (Time Study survey, Fig. D-11), renormalized (SOURCE_NOTES E6).

demand.carlessRideshareShare.note: 86.9% of people without a vehicle ride with someone else (Time Study 3-9). In the simulator they ride with an evacuating household on the same street; the rest are stranded (SOURCE_NOTES E7).

demand.compliance.note: Share of households that leave: 100% in Order zones, 50% in Warning zones, 20% shadow/voluntary elsewhere (Time Study 2-3, 7-1, from NUREG/CR-7002) (SOURCE_NOTES E8). Shadow evacuees drive to the city edge.

demand.childPickupShare.note: Share of households that pick up children when school is in session (switches to Time Study distributions E/F). Placeholder; ACS households with children would replace it.

demand.mobilization15min.note: Percent of trips starting in each 15-minute period after the order, Time Study Table 5-9 (p. 5-14) (SOURCE_NOTES E9). A employees/visitors; C residents awaiting a returning commuter (also used for shadow evacuees); D residents not awaiting one; E/F = C/D with child pickup.

parking.range.note: Parking varies by block and by seed. On hill blocks wide enough for both sides: noParkingShareHills parked on neither side, oneSideShareHills on one side, the rest on both (City 2020 aerial counts of 22 hill blocks, data/field/aerial-parking-counts-2020.json: of 12 wider blocks 2 had none, 4 one side, 6 both on at least part; on blocks of 22 ft or less 7 of 9 were one side or sparse, which the 8 ft rule below already produces). offPavementShare / offPavementSavesM: share of hill blocks where cars sit partly off the pavement and the width that saves (Poppy Ln, Latham Ln photos). minLeftForCarsM: residents stop parking where less than 8 ft would remain for a car (City Narrow_Roads shows 7-8 ft left on many streets). curbMPerCar: one parked car per this many meters of a parked side (aerial counts: about 19 m in daytime; 15 assumed to allow for fuller evenings). badJobPerCar, badJobExtraM: each parked car has a small chance of being a bad job (wide vehicle or far from the curb) that narrows the gap by 1.5-4 ft (red van photo); not measurable from the aerials. Placeholders until curb data or evening counts.

sharedLane.note: Two-way streets with one moving lane between parked cars: both directions share one lane's capacity. When both directions have traffic, drivers take turns at gaps (driveways) every passingGapM; each switch loses about passingGapM / speed + 3 s against platoonS of flow. Below one 10 ft lane flow is cut by squeezeBelowLaneFactor; below crawlBelowM (7 ft) cars creep through at crawlFactor. Placeholders until gap spacing is counted from aerial photos. opposingWaitS: in route choice, each oncoming car on a one-lane street counts as this much delay, so drivers avoid turning into oncoming traffic (without it, re-routing around hill loops created two-way jams on Panoramic Hill).

demand.returnDriveMin.note: Households awaiting a returning commuter (Time Study distributions C and E): the commuter leaves work on the Time Study employee curve (Table 5-9 A), then drives this many minutes (uniform range) to reach the edge of the evacuating area, then drives home on Berkeley streets against the outbound traffic. Their car is one of the household's vehicles, so it adds an inbound trip but no extra outbound vehicle. A commuter turned back by fire leaves the household one car short. Workplace locations are not modeled.

capacity.gridlockReliefS.note: A vehicle that has waited this long at the head of a queue squeezes into a full downstream link, and an oncoming car stuck this long no longer holds up the other direction on a take-turns street. Prevents permanent lock-ups that a simple queue model creates in rings such as traffic circles. Each use is counted in the run summary.

nonResident.note: Vehicle counts from the 2025 Evacuation Time Study: employees by area (Table 3-5), college students (Tables 3-8, 3-9), visitors including 549 at Tilden lots (§3.5), I-80 through traffic over 2 h after the order (Table 3-12); scaled by the scenario's percent present (Table 6-5) (SOURCE_NOTES E32-E36). Placement is a model rule: the study's areas are approximated from City neighborhoods (West Berkeley = 4th St., Gilman, NW/SW Berkeley, Marina), fire zones (hills north/south of campus), LBNL employees on streets in the Lab's zones (LBL-*), 400 m around Berkeley City College, streets within 1 km of the campus center, outside the campus and outside Fire Zones 2-3, for commuting students; visitors on streets outside Fire Zones 2-3, 400 m around two Tilden entrances (approximate points), weighted by street length. The I-80 and CA-24 westbound (the study's "SB") parts of the study's through traffic are on our network; I-580 and I-880 lie outside the model area except where I-580 shares the I-80 freeway.

intersections.delayS.note: Average delay per junction when traffic is light, added to the travel time into each junction: about 20 s at arterial junctions (mostly signals; HCM uncongested signal delay is typically 10-35 s), 10 s on collectors, 5 s on local streets (stop signs, yielding). The street file has no signal or stop-sign data; the Time Study models each signal. Set once from typical values, not tuned.

intersections.scale.note: Multiplier on collector and arterial intersection capacities (local and freeway junctions unchanged). The one setting tuned against the Time Study (1923 repeat, night S3 and fall weekday S4); checked on cases not used for tuning. See SOURCE_NOTES calibration.

parking.range.night.note: Night cases (Time Study S3, S6): residents are home, so fewer hill blocks have no parked cars and parked sides are fuller (one car per 9 m instead of 15 m), which raises the chance of a bad parking job. Placeholder until evening counts or curb data; daytime aerial counts found about one car per 19 m. Suggested in pasted egress notes (SOURCE_NOTES P3) and consistent with Eric's photos being daytime.

intersections.circleVph.note: Traffic circles at about 900 veh/h per lane (Time Study Appendix G, SOURCE_NOTES E16), applied to network nodes inside OpenStreetMap junction=roundabout rings.

access.barrierDelayS.note: Time for an engine crew to open a gate or remove an emergency bollard (3 min, middle of the 2-5 min in pasted egress notes, SOURCE_NOTES P2; unsourced).

population.overrides.note: Per zone, "census2020" replaces the Genasys estimate with the 2020 Census count of the blocks whose interior point lies in the zone (Census TIGERweb, POP100). Eric's choices, 2026-11-01: OKL-003 (Claremont Canyon, an R04 Panoramic Hill order zone) uses 307 instead of the Genasys estimate of 27 (SOURCE_NOTES X6); BER-013 (Panoramic Hill, the part in Oakland, an R04 order zone; Genasys outline per Z1) uses 122 instead of the Genasys estimate of 83 (SOURCE_NOTES Z2).

network.osmAdditions.note: Roads added from OpenStreetMap that the street extract leaves out because OSM tags them highway=service (Overpass API, 2026-11-01; © OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL; query in data/raw/osm/lbnl-gate-roads.overpassql). The County street file stops the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory's streets at the city line, so the model's Lab had one way out, Cyclotron Rd to Hearst Av (the Blackberry Canyon Entrance). OSM continues McMillan Road to the Grizzly Peak Gate and Lawrence Road to the Strawberry Canyon Gate, both on Centennial Dr. Geometry, names and one-way tags are sourced; using the gates as exits is a model rule: the Lab's gates are staffed and private (access=private), and the simulator opens all three to cars leaving the Lab, the same rule it already applied to the two Grizzly Peak Gate pieces in the street extract (meta.barrierSites, keptOpen). Each entry is matched by way and node ids; the builder stops if they no longer exist. Edges carry src.added. SOURCE_NOTES Z5.

network.labGatesExitOnly.note: The Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory's streets are private (OpenStreetMap access=private) and its three gates (Blackberry Canyon Entrance on Cyclotron Rd, Grizzly Peak Gate and Strawberry Canyon Gate on Centennial Dr) are staffed. In an evacuation the simulator lets cars leave the Lab by any gate and lets none drive in, so no outside traffic cuts through the Lab between Hearst Av and Centennial Dr (with the gates open both ways, 24 Northside cars did in the 1923 repeat, weekday S4, seed 1). Engines still pass. How the Lab actually runs its gates in an evacuation is an information gap. SOURCE_NOTES Z5.

growth.options.note: Future growth (Scenario, shared by both plans). Unit counts are the Time Study's (sourced) except the moderate case (assumption). Each added unit is a synthetic household drawn like today's: 2.37 persons (the Time Study's figure for ADUs too) and the same vehicle shares, about 1.12 vehicles per unit against the study's 1.14 (30,848 ÷ 27,060). Parked cars do not change with growth.

growth.allocation.note: The Time Study gives one Hillside Overlay total, with no split by region or street. Units go to Berkeley's Fire Zones 2–3 (standing in for the Hillside Overlay, which the study says encompasses the Very High Fire Hazard Severity Zone; no City GIS layer of the overlay was found) in proportion to each street's share of today's households, since eligible parcels are existing homes. Placement depends on the seed only, so both plans see the same added homes.

growth.r0Areas.note: R0 (plan setting, Eric 2026-11-01): no added units in a chosen area. It removes only the growth placed there and does not count homes lost to fire as people moving out. Legal status per SOURCE_NOTES L1–L9.

routing.forecastMarginMin.note: Constrained egress guidance (plan setting Driver information and routing): a street counts as in the forecast ember or fire area if the illustrative fire's embers or front reach it within this many minutes from now. The forecast is the simulator's own fire, so it is never wrong; a real forecast would be uncertain, and a wider margin is the stand-in for that uncertainty. SOURCE_NOTES DG8.

routing.timeToleranceS.note: Constrained egress guidance offers a load-balancing route only if, for that driver, it is expected (at current queues) to take no more than this many seconds longer than the driver's own best route, and spends no more time in the forecast ember area. SOURCE_NOTES DG8.

routing.emberSecondWeight.note: Constrained egress guidance ranks routes by safety first: each second driven in the forecast ember area counts as this many seconds of travel, and any street in the forecast fire area is avoided whenever another way out exists. SOURCE_NOTES DG8.

routing.systemQueueWeight.note: Load balancing (constrained guidance and the unconstrained system-optimal comparison): a car's route cost counts its queue delay (1 + this) times, a simple stand-in for the delay it adds to the cars queued behind it (marginal cost). Re-planned every minute on current queues, not forecast ones. SOURCE_NOTES DG9.

routing.worseOffDelayMin.note: Households worse off (Compare, plans that differ in routing): a household counts as worse off under Plan B if it is still there when embers or the fire front reach it, or cut off, where it was not under Plan A, or if it reaches safety more than this many minutes later. Runs are paired by seed; households by identity. SOURCE_NOTES DG10.

network.segmentCorrections.note: County street-file records corrected where other sources show the County coding is wrong, each on Eric's decision; each is matched by SEGID and OBJECTID, sets the listed County fields before the network is built, and is listed in network.meta.segmentCorrections and on the edge (correction), with its sources in the entry's why. (1) Eric, 2026-11-01: the 45 m link from the foot of Panoramic Way to Prospect St / Canyon Rd (County OBJECTID 25386, SEGID 181025458, "BANCROFT STEPS WY", TRVLWAY NT) is a two-way street. OpenStreetMap maps it as Bancroft Way (way 24025453, highway=tertiary, lanes=2, no access or oneway tags, checked 2026-11-01); the City Street_Centerline layer has it as pavement section 627042086 (Seg-00193, Prospect St to Panoramic Way, 30 ft, 2 lanes, two-way); the City's AB 747 street layer gives it a capacity of 1,125 vehicles/h; the SB 99 report (KLD, Rev. 3, p. 4) puts Panoramic Hill's single access point at "Panoramic Way and Prospect St/Canyon Rd". The Bancroft Steps stairway is a separate feature (OSM ways 311861379-311861382 and 24025452, motor_vehicle=no, Warring St to Prospect St) and is not in the County file. SOURCE_NOTES K1-K6. (2) Eric, 2026-11-01, choosing between conflicting sources: The Crossways (County OBJECTID 35701, SEGID 181035806, 67 m, Overlook Rd to Middlefield Rd, TRVLWAY NT) is a two-way street, as OpenStreetMap (way 6391261, residential, with a stop sign), the City pavement records (Seg-02488, 21 ft, 2 lanes), the City Narrow_Roads survey and KLD's AB 747 model (capacity 1,125 veh/h) have it; the County record and the City segment's network fields (CATEGORY PEDESTRIAN, NET_CFCC A72 stairway) code it a walkway. SOURCE_NOTES K5, K8.

operations.contraflow.note: Contraflow start-up (SOURCE_NOTES CF3–CF6). Pre-installed signs and gates, rehearsed: they switch on 10 min after the zone's order (time to switch them and let the last inbound cars clear; the MUTCD requires the red X long enough for the lane to clear, §4T.04). Mechanical fallback (gates swung and signs unfolded by hand): 15 min more. Officer-staffed: one officer per entry point; no public source gives a staffing ratio. For scale, Paradise's 2016 drill ran Skyway one-way out between 07:00 and 08:00, and in the 2018 Camp Fire Clark Rd ran four lanes out by 09:00 (NIST TN 2252, pp. 38, 92).

operations.contraflow.costPerEntryUSD.note: Capital cost per entry point, US dollars: low, one LED blank-out sign furnished and installed ($6,985, City of La Vista, NE, council report, 2024-04-16); high, one single-faced lane-use control signal ($32,000–$50,000, 2019, USDOT ITS cost database, read from a search excerpt, not verified). Battery backup adds about $7,000 for a complete system (City of Eastvale, CA, FY2023-24 capital plan). Gates are not costed: the only figure found is $100,000–$150,000 per location in 1995 dollars (ITS database, not verified). No public unit cost was found for mechanical fold-out signs and swing gates.

operations.police.officers.note: Officer pool for contraflow and junctions: 10, 20, 40 or 80. For scale (sourced): Berkeley Police had 154 sworn officers filled, 144 available, 174 authorized in 2025 (BPD 2025 Annual Report, slide 4); patrol minimum staffing was 60 sworn officers in 7 teams of 4 to 9 (City memo, 2022-05-05), and a 2026 patrol schedule has about 7 or 8 per team (Berkeley Scanner, 2026-04-14, quoting police); UC Berkeley Police had 49 sworn officers (August 2025). Officers on duty at any one time are roughly one or two teams; more need callback or mutual aid. Officers per junction: 1 (assumption). Arrival delay 15, 30 or 60 min after the first order (assumption).

operations.police.capacityUplift.note: An officer-controlled junction passes 9% more vehicles than its model capacity and serves approaches heading toward safety first. 9% is the high end of published findings: manual control 'increased intersection capacity by as much as 9 percent' at oversaturated isolated intersections (Mahalel, Gur and Shiftan 1991, cited in Parr and Wolshon, SWUTC/15/600451-00113-1, 2015, p. 30); the same report measured about equal throughput and longer delays with an officer than with an actuated signal (pp. 84–88), and a 2020 simulation of evacuations found manual control gave no significant benefit and longer clearance in dense areas (Parr, Herrera, Wolshon and Smith, TRR 2674(9)). The Time Study models staffed control as actuated timing (§4.3, p. 4-7); converting pre-timed signals to actuated cut its evacuation times by up to 13% (p. 10-9).

operations.powerShutoff.note: Which signals go dark (SOURCE_NOTES CF10–CF12): 'hills' darkens the 30 City signals at junctions on or within 150 m of a Fire Zones 2–3 street (tools/signals.mjs), standing in for the hill circuits PG&E shut off on 26–28 October 2019 (Arlington, Ridge and Substations F, G and K circuits in Tier 2 or 3 fire-threat areas; PG&E post-event report to the CPUC, appendix pp. 77–91); 'all' darkens all 146. No public source says which Berkeley signals have battery backup; the Time Study recommends adding 6–8 hours of it to every cabinet (Rec. 8.2), so none is assumed. Caltrans says signals on battery run normally for about 3 hours, then flash red (District 11, 2025-01-07); the 2019 shutoff lasted about 39 to 46 hours.

operations.powerShutoff.allWayStopVph.note: A dark signal is an all-way stop (California Vehicle Code §21800(d)). Capacity about 900 vehicles per hour through the junction: the HCM's base saturation headway at a single-lane all-way stop is 3.9 s (Exhibit 21-15, as reproduced in the NCHRP 08-135 guidebook), about 920 per hour, and the Time Study gives traffic circles, 'often functioning as all-way stops', about 900 vehicles per hour per lane (App. G, p. G-1). A junction whose model capacity is already lower keeps it.

operations.contraflow.reversedLaneFactor.note: The reversed lane carries 70% of a normal lane's capacity. On I-55 during the Hurricane Katrina evacuation the contraflow lanes peaked at 1,842 vehicles per hour, 'about 30 percent lower than the adjacent normal-flow lanes' (Wolshon, 'Empirical Characterization of Mass Evacuation Traffic Flow', TRB 2008 preprint 08-0930, pp. 9–10). Freeway data; no figure for two-lane streets was found.

none.label: None (today's population)
none.note: Residents as today: Genasys zone estimates (2020 Census where Genasys has none).

middle.label: Middle housing only (Time Study: 870 units)
middle.note: Time Study §10.5.3 and Table 10-11 (pp. 10-7, 10-17): 6,440 Hillside Overlay parcels × 4.5% likely to develop by 2031 × 3 units = 870 units (2,062 people, 992 vehicles), under the middle-housing zoning the study evaluated. Whether Berkeley's adopted middle-housing rules apply in the Hillside Overlay was not checked.

moderate.label: Moderate ADU growth (assumption: 2,706 units, 10% of the maximum)
moderate.note: Assumption: 10% of the Time Study's maximum. Berkeley permitted 95 to 123 ADUs a year citywide in 2021 and 2023 to 2025 (Housing Element Annual Progress Reports to HCD; no count for the hills alone was found), so 2,706 units is about 25 years of the citywide pace even if every ADU were built in the hills.

max.label: Maximum ADU build-out (Time Study: 27,060 units)
max.note: Time Study §10.5.2 and Table 10-11 (pp. 10-6, 10-17): about 9,020 eligible Hillside Overlay parcels × (2 ADUs + 1 JADU) = 27,060 units, 64,132 people, 30,848 vehicles. The study calls it the maximum theoretical build-out under HCD's reading of state law; it is not a forecast.

growth.allocation: Berkeley Fire Zones 2–3, by each street's share of today's households

r0.none: R0 is off: added homes are built wherever Future growth (Scenario) puts them.

areas.lez: No added homes in the City's 10 Leave Early Zones (Upper Hills, Panoramic Hill), about 29% of the modeled build-out. Growth elsewhere in the hills goes ahead; none moves.
areas.fz23: No added homes in Berkeley's Fire Zones 2–3. All modeled growth sits there, so this removes all of it.
areas.access: No added homes on streets behind a choke point (a street or one-way piece whose loss cuts them off from every exit; tools/access-constraints.mjs), about 11% of the modeled build-out.

r0.legal: Current law lets Berkeley bar ADUs beyond the state's by-right minimum in designated areas, with ADU-specific findings on traffic and public safety (Gov. Code §66314(a); HCD ADU Handbook, March 2026, pp. 42–43), and deny single SB 9 projects case by case (§65852.21(d)). Each single-family lot keeps a by-right conversion ADU, an 800 sq ft detached ADU and a JADU (§66323), which is all of the Time Study's maximum, so barring those units or SB 9 across an area would need a change in state law or an HCD-approved moratorium on an imminent-threat finding (§66300(b)(1)(B)).
r0.provenance: Model rule: R0 removes the added homes on streets in the chosen area and moves none elsewhere. Areas: Leave Early Zones and Fire Zones 2–3 from City sources; access-constrained areas derived from the street network. Legal status: sourced from the Government Code, HCD's ADU Handbook and HCD's letters to Berkeley (2022, 2026); which units are by-right is our reading of §66323 (SOURCE_NOTES L1–L9).

segmentCorrections.why: Drivable two-way link from the foot of Panoramic Way to Prospect St / Canyon Rd, Panoramic Hill's single exit (SB 99, p. 4). OSM: Bancroft Way, tertiary, 2 lanes, no access restriction; City Street_Centerline Seg-00193: 30 ft, 2 lanes, two-way. The County record codes it no vehicle travel and names it after the Bancroft Steps stairway, which runs from Warring St to Prospect St and is a separate feature. SOURCE_NOTES K1-K6.

Eric, 2026-11-01, choosing between conflicting sources: The Crossways, a 67 m link from Overlook Rd to Middlefield Rd, is a two-way street. For a street: OSM way 6391261 (highway=residential, surface=asphalt, no access tag, stop sign node 10819110534 on the way; an unreviewed TIGER import), the City Street_Centerline pavement fields for Seg-02488 (pavement section THE CROSSWAYS, Overlook Rd to Middlefield Rd, 21 ft, 2 lanes), the City Narrow_Roads survey (Link_ID 1503, 21 ft) and the City's AB 747 street layer (KLD's model: capacity 1,125 veh/h, volume-to-capacity 0.41-0.44). Against: the County record (TRVLWAY NT) and the network fields of the same City segment (CATEGORY PEDESTRIAN, NET_CFCC A72 stairway, drive times -1). SOURCE_NOTES K5, K8.

osmAdditions.why: McMillan Road from the County file's end of McMillian Rd (County node at -122.24513, 37.87698) to the Grizzly Peak Gate pair (OSM gate nodes 462036035 and 5843474846) that leads to Centennial Dr. About 90 m; OSM highway=service, access=private.
Lawrence Road from the County file's end of Lee Rd (-122.24597, 37.87522) east to the Strawberry Canyon Gate on Centennial Dr. About 700 m; OSM highway=service, access=private, bus=yes.
Strawberry Canyon Gate, outbound: one-way from Lawrence Road to Centennial Dr (OSM gate node 7782319497).
Strawberry Canyon Gate, inbound: one-way from Centennial Dr to Lawrence Road (OSM gate node 7782302882).
